questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: A spreadsheet cell contains 2170. Which additional fact would be sufficient to classify it as ratio data?
options: It is the number of litres of fuel purchased in a transaction
It is the postcode of the customer's billing address
It is stored as a number rather than as text
It is the year in which the account was opened
questions.explanation: Ratio requires a true zero, so arithmetic including ratios is meaningful — zero litres means none. A postcode is nominal, a calendar year is interval (year 0 is arbitrary), and the storage type is irrelevant to the level of measurement.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which pair of values could not validly be averaged?
options: Response times in seconds for 40 support tickets
Daily maximum temperatures in degrees Celsius across a month
Annual revenue figures for six branches
Customer satisfaction recorded as Poor / Fair / Good / Excellent
questions.explanation: Ordinal categories have order but unequal intervals, so the mean assumes a precision the data does not carry. Celsius is interval — the mean is valid even though ratios are not, which is the distinction most often confused here.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: An enterprise argues that because star ratings are stored as integers 1–5, the mean rating is a valid KPI. The strongest counter is:
options: The intervals between adjacent ratings are not demonstrably equal, so the mean implies a precision the scale lacks
Ratings must be converted to percentages before any statistic is calculated
Star ratings are nominal, so only the mode may be reported
The mean is only valid for continuous data, and integers are discrete
questions.explanation: Star ratings are ordinal. They are not nominal — the order is real — which is why (C) overstates the objection, and the discrete/continuous distinction in (D) is a separate issue that does not by itself invalidate a mean.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of information rather than data?
options: A log file containing 40,000 timestamped page requests
The value 00:04:12 recorded against session 88214
"Average session duration fell 18% after the checkout redesign"
A database table of every completed transaction this quarter
questions.explanation: Information is data processed, organised and given context so it carries meaning. The others are raw facts — large volume does not make data into information, which is the trap in (A) and (D).

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: In the DIKW model, the step from knowledge to wisdom is best characterised as:
options: Applying judgement about what should be done, including when not to act
Aggregating individual records into summary statistics
Adding context so the data becomes meaningful
Storing the processed output in a data warehouse for reuse
questions.explanation: Data → information adds context, information → knowledge adds understanding of patterns and causes, knowledge → wisdom adds judgement and values. (C) describes the first step, not the last.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which dataset is semi-structured?
options: An XML feed where optional elements appear only in some records
A normalised relational table with enforced data types
A folder of scanned invoices stored as JPEG images
A CSV export with a fixed header row and consistent columns
questions.explanation: Semi-structured data carries tags or markers but no rigid schema. A CSV is structured despite being a flat file — the trap is assuming "not a database" means "not structured".

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: An enterprise says 85% of its data is unstructured. The most significant analytical consequence is:
options: The data cannot be stored economically
The data has no metadata and therefore cannot be catalogued
SQL alone cannot interrogate it, so NLP, computer vision or ML techniques are required
The data must be discarded after its retention period expires
questions.explanation: Unstructured data usually has rich metadata, so (B) is false. Storage is cheap; the barrier is that the query tools most enterprises own cannot read it.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which variable is interval rather than ratio?
options: Time taken to complete a task, in minutes
Weight of a parcel in kilograms
Number of items in a shopping basket
IQ score
questions.explanation: IQ — The scale has order and (by construction) equal intervals, but its zero is arbitrary — an IQ of 140 is not "twice as intelligent" as 70. The others all have a genuine zero.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: A researcher codes free-text complaints into themes and counts how often each theme appears. The resulting counts are:
options: Qualitative data, because the source material was qualitative
Quantitative data at the nominal level, since the themes are unordered labels being counted
Ordinal data, because some themes are more serious than others
Invalid, because qualitative data cannot be counted
questions.explanation: Thematic coding produces nominal categories, and frequency counts of those categories are legitimate quantitative analysis. (A) is the common error — the analysis, not the source, determines the type.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: The strongest justification for a mixed-methods approach is that:
options: Quantitative data establishes what is happening while qualitative data explains why
It doubles the sample size and therefore halves the margin of error
Qualitative data is more reliable than quantitative data
It satisfies the requirement to collect both active and passive data
questions.explanation: (B) confuses two separate datasets with one larger sample, and (D) invents a requirement — active/passive is a collection taxonomy, not a methodological obligation.

questions.stem: A hotel places a tablet at reception inviting departing guests to rate their stay. This is:
options: Computerised and passive, because a device records the response
Manual and passive, because no interviewer is present
Manual and active, because a staff member prompts the guest
Computerised and active, because the guest knowingly participates
questions.explanation: The axis is knowing participation, not whether a human is present. The device makes it computerised; the guest's deliberate response makes it active.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of passive collection for an enterprise investigating why customers churn?
options: The data volume is too small to support statistical analysis
It requires explicit consent from every customer before collection
It cannot be timestamped, so trends cannot be established
It records behaviour but cannot capture motivation or reasoning
questions.explanation: Passive collection typically produces more data, not less, and it is routinely timestamped. Its structural gap is the missing why — which is exactly what a churn investigation needs.

questions.stem: An enterprise samples every 20th customer from a list sorted by signup date. The specific risk is:
options: Periodic bias, if a cycle in the list coincides with the sampling interval
Volunteer bias, since customers self-select into the sample
Coverage bias, since the sampling frame excludes non-customers
Response bias, since customers may answer to please the interviewer
questions.explanation: This is systematic sampling. (C) is true of any customer list but is not caused by the method; the method-specific hazard is a periodic pattern aligning with the interval.

questions.stem: A researcher needs to guarantee that a 4% minority group is represented proportionally. The correct method is:
options: Stratified sampling with the group as its own stratum
Simple random sampling with a large enough sample
Cluster sampling by geographic region
Systematic sampling with a small interval
questions.explanation: Random sampling makes proportional representation likely but does not guarantee it — that word is what rules out (B). Stratification enforces it by construction.

questions.stem: Cluster sampling is chosen primarily because it:
options: Reduces cost and logistical difficulty when the population is geographically dispersed
Produces a smaller margin of error than simple random sampling
Removes the need for a sampling frame entirely
Guarantees each subgroup is represented in proportion to its size
questions.explanation: It trades precision for practicality — members within a cluster tend to be similar, so sampling error is higher for the same sample size, which is the opposite of (B).

questions.stem: Which finding would most strongly indicate a problem with validity rather than reliability?
options: Two researchers using the same instrument produce different results
The survey measures brand awareness but is being used to conclude purchase intent
The instrument produces the same wrong reading every time
Repeating the survey next month produces very different answers
questions.explanation: Validity is about measuring the right construct. (A) and (D) are reliability failures, and (C) is the classic reliable-but-inaccurate case.

questions.stem: A dataset is highly accurate and highly reliable but was collected in 2015 for a question about current behaviour. The failing criterion is:
options: Reliability
Accuracy
Relevance
Validity
questions.explanation: Relevance — whether the data actually relates to the question being asked. Age is a relevance problem here rather than an accuracy one; the 2015 figures may be perfectly correct for 2015.

questions.stem: Which is a transposition error rather than a transcription error?
options: Entering Smith as Smyth
Entering $1,450 as $14,50
Leaving a required field blank
Entering 4821 as 4281
questions.explanation: Transposition = characters swapped. (B) is a misplaced separator and (A) a mistyping — both transcription errors. Check digits are designed specifically to catch (D).

questions.stem: A "presence check" would catch which of the following?
options: A price entered as twelve dollars
An email address entered without an @
A date of birth of 2099-01-01
A required phone number field left empty
questions.explanation: Presence = is there anything here. (C) needs a range check, (B) a format check and (A) a type check — all four are validation, which is why the distractors are close.

questions.stem: Validation confirms an entered customer address is correctly formatted and plausible. It cannot confirm that:
options: The postcode field contains four digits
The address is the one where the customer actually lives
The state field contains a recognised abbreviation
The field is not empty
questions.explanation: Validation tests form and reasonableness, not truth. Confirming the value matches the source is verification, and confirming it matches reality needs an external check.

questions.stem: A sensor drifts out of calibration and records every reading 4% high. This is best described as:
options: An outlier problem requiring winsorisation
Random error, which cancels out across a large sample
Systematic measurement bias, which does not cancel out
A transcription error introduced at the data entry stage
questions.explanation: The critical property is that a systematic offset persists no matter how large the sample grows — which is precisely why (B) is wrong and why more data does not fix bias.

questions.stem: An analyst removes all values more than three standard deviations from the mean before reporting. The strongest objection is:
options: Standard deviation cannot be calculated on ratio data
The rule may delete genuine extremes that carry the most important signal, and the deletion is undocumented
Outliers should always be replaced with the median instead
Three standard deviations is too wide a threshold to remove anything
questions.explanation: Fraud, equipment failure and the best customer all look like outliers. The defensible practice is investigate, decide, and document — not apply a rule silently.

questions.stem: Which is confirmation bias rather than selection bias?
options: Excluding records with missing values without checking why they are missing
Surveying only customers who opened the marketing email
Recruiting participants at a shopping centre on a weekday morning
Stopping data collection once the results support the expected conclusion
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias operates on the analyst's decisions about evidence. (B) and (C) shape the sample; (A) is a cleaning decision that can create bias but is not confirmation bias.

questions.stem: Records with missing income values turn out to be concentrated among low-income respondents. Deleting those rows would:
options: Have no effect, since the remaining data is complete
Reduce reliability but not introduce bias
Introduce bias, because the missingness is related to the value itself
Be acceptable provided the deletion is documented
questions.explanation: Missingness that correlates with the underlying value is not random, so deleting shifts the distribution. Documentation (D) is necessary but does not repair the distortion.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of metadata creating a privacy risk without any content being exposed?
options: A leaked spreadsheet of customer email addresses
A published dashboard of aggregate regional sales
Call records showing who contacted a crisis helpline, when, and from where
A backup file encrypted with an outdated algorithm
questions.explanation: No conversation content is revealed, yet the pattern is highly sensitive and identifying. (A) is content, not metadata — the distinction the question tests.

questions.stem: A dataset described as "primary" for one enterprise becomes "secondary" when:
options: It is more than 12 months old
It is reused by a different party for a different purpose
It is aggregated to protect privacy
It is transferred into a data warehouse
questions.explanation: Primary/secondary describes the relationship between the collector and the user, not the age, location or state of processing of the data.

questions.stem: A convenience sample of 12,000 responses and a random sample of 800 both address the same question. The random sample is preferable because:
options: Smaller samples are less prone to data entry error
Sample size cannot compensate for a sample that is systematically unrepresentative
Random sampling removes response bias as well as selection bias
Convenience samples cannot be analysed statistically
questions.explanation: This is the central lesson of sampling: bias does not shrink with n. (C) overclaims — random selection addresses who is chosen, not how honestly they answer.

questions.stem: Which action would most improve the reliability of a data collection instrument?
options: Increasing the sample size
Adding an open-ended comment field
Cross-checking a subset of records against an authoritative source
Standardising the wording, order and administration of every question
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency on repetition, so it is improved by controlling the procedure. (C) improves accuracy, and (A) affects precision of estimates rather than instrument consistency.

questions.stem: An enterprise cleans a dataset by standardising "NSW", "N.S.W." and "New South Wales" to a single value. This is:
options: Data cleaning through standardisation of formats
Verification, since values are checked against the source
Validation, since inconsistent values are rejected
De-identification, since the specific value is generalised
questions.explanation: Nothing is rejected and nothing is checked against a source, which rules out the first two; and generalising a state does not de-identify anyone.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that a survey suffers from response bias?
options: The response rate was 8%
Self-reported exercise minutes far exceed measured activity for the same respondents
Responses were collected only through the mobile app
Some respondents skipped the income question
questions.explanation: A measurable gap between reported and actual behaviour is direct evidence. (A) and (C) point to non-response and coverage bias, and (D) to item non-response.

questions.stem: Altering a transaction in block 2 of a five-block chain is detectable because:
options: Each block is encrypted with the network's shared private key
Block 3 stores block 2's hash, which no longer matches, and the mismatch cascades forward
The blockchain automatically restores the original value from a backup node
Every block stores a complete copy of all previous blocks
questions.explanation: Blockchain data is typically hashed and often public, not encrypted for secrecy, which is why (A) is wrong; and blocks store only the previous hash, not the full history, ruling out (D).

questions.stem: The property that makes a hash useful for integrity checking is that it is:
options: Reversible with the correct key
Fixed-length and one-way, with any input change producing a different output
Unique to each user, like a private key
Compressed, so large files can be reconstructed from it
questions.explanation: (D) is the classic misconception — a hash is not compression, and the original cannot be recovered from it.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants tamper-evident records but is the sole party controlling the data. The best advice is:
options: Use a data lake, since raw data preserves the original state
Adopt blockchain, since immutability is always preferable
Use a conventional database with cryptographic audit logging, since blockchain's cost is justified by distrust between parties
Use a data warehouse, since ETL creates an audit trail
questions.explanation: Blockchain's value proposition is trust between parties who do not trust each other. With a single controlling party, its throughput and energy costs buy little that signed audit logs do not.

questions.stem: A smart contract poses which distinctive enterprise risk?
options: It cannot be executed without human approval
It cannot record the outcome of its own execution
It requires all nodes to hold identical private keys
A defect in its logic is as immutable as the data it operates on
questions.explanation: Immutability cuts both ways — the property that makes the record trustworthy makes the bug permanent, which is why formal review before deployment matters so much.

questions.stem: Which enterprise problem is a velocity problem rather than a volume problem?
options: Ten years of transaction history no longer fits on the existing server
Fraud must be detected before a card authorisation completes
Data arrives as a mix of video, free text and sensor readings
Two source systems define "active customer" differently
questions.explanation: Velocity is about the speed of generation and required processing. (A) is volume, (C) variety and (D) veracity/governance.

questions.stem: The characteristic that distinguishes a data lake from a data warehouse is that the lake:
options: Contains only a single department's subject area
Cannot store unstructured data
Is always hosted on premises rather than in the cloud
Stores data in its native raw format with schema applied on read
questions.explanation: Schema-on-read versus schema-on-write is the structural difference. (A) describes a data mart, and (B) inverts the lake's main advantage.

questions.stem: During ETL, which activity belongs to Transform rather than Load?
options: Indexing the target tables after insertion
Writing conformed records into the fact table
Reconciling currency units and deduplicating customer records
Reading rows from the source CRM system
questions.explanation: Transform is where cleaning, standardising, conforming and aggregating happen — and where invisible editorial decisions get baked into every downstream chart.

questions.stem: A supermarket wants to know which customer segments exist in its transaction data, without knowing the segments in advance. The technique is:
options: Classification, using labelled historical segments
Regression, which predicts a numeric value
Association analysis, which finds co-occurring items
Clustering, which finds groupings in unlabelled data
questions.explanation: The phrase "without knowing the segments in advance" rules out classification, which requires predefined labels — that is the intended trap.

questions.stem: An insurer builds a model to predict claim cost in dollars. This is:
options: Classification
Association
Clustering
Regression
questions.explanation: Regression — a continuous numeric output. Predicting whether a claim will be made would be classification, which is how these two are usually confused.

questions.stem: Market basket analysis reports that bread and milk co-occur in 60% of baskets. The most defensible conclusion is:
options: The two are frequently purchased together, which may reflect that both are staples rather than any relationship between them
Moving milk next to bread will increase milk sales by 60%
Buying bread causes customers to buy milk
Customers who buy milk will buy bread 60% of the time
questions.explanation: High-support pairs of staples are often trivially co-occurring. (D) also misreads the statistic — support is not the same as confidence in a given direction.

questions.stem: Anomaly detection's primary business cost is:
options: It cannot operate on streaming data
False positives that block legitimate customers
It requires labelled training data for every fraud type
It can only run in batch, so detection is always retrospective
questions.explanation: The detection threshold is a business decision balancing missed fraud against customer harm — not a purely technical one.

questions.stem: Which is data mining rather than querying?
options: Producing this month's sales report by region
Calculating the total value of outstanding invoices
Filtering the customer table for accounts over 12 months old
Discovering that customers who change address are three times more likely to lapse
questions.explanation: Mining discovers previously unknown patterns. Running a report you already designed — however large the dataset — is querying.

questions.stem: A data mart's most significant governance risk is:
options: It cannot be refreshed from the warehouse
It stores raw unprocessed data indefinitely
Departments drift into conflicting definitions of the same measure
It cannot enforce access controls
questions.explanation: The "one version of the truth" problem re-emerges at the mart level, which is why conformed dimensions matter.

questions.stem: A retailer keeps every raw web clickstream event for seven years "in case it becomes useful". The strongest criticism is:
options: Clickstream data cannot be analysed after 12 months
Retention beyond five years is prohibited under the Privacy Act
Raw data cannot be stored in a data lake
It increases storage cost and privacy exposure without a stated purpose, contrary to data minimisation
questions.explanation: (B) invents a fixed statutory limit — the APPs require destruction when the data is no longer needed, not after a set number of years.

questions.stem: Which of the "extra two Vs" is most directly a trust question?
options: Veracity
Variety
Volume
Value
questions.explanation: Veracity — the accuracy, integrity and credibility of the data. Value asks whether the data is worth holding at all, which is the adjacent concept being tested.

questions.stem: A junction table resolving a M:N relationship between DOCTOR and PATIENT should have a primary key that is:
options: A new auto-generated ID with no relationship to either table
PatientID alone, since a patient is the subject of the record
The composite of DoctorID and PatientID, both of which are also foreign keys
DoctorID alone, since a doctor sees many patients
questions.explanation: Either single key would allow only one row per doctor or per patient, destroying the many-to-many. A surrogate key (A) is workable in practice but is not what the syllabus expects, and it loses the uniqueness constraint unless separately enforced.

questions.stem: Referential integrity would prevent which of the following?
options: Deleting a customer who still has orders referencing them
Entering a customer's phone number in the email field
Storing two customers with the same surname
Entering a date of birth in the future
questions.explanation: Referential integrity governs relationships between tables. (B) and (D) are validation problems and (C) is not an error at all — surnames are not unique.

questions.stem: Which query returns one row per suburb?
options: SELECT Suburb FROM Customer;
SELECT Suburb FROM Customer ORDER BY Suburb;
SELECT DISTINCT Suburb, CustomerID FROM Customer;
SELECT Suburb, COUNT(*) FROM Customer GROUP BY Suburb;
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows to one per distinct suburb. (C) is the trap — adding CustomerID to DISTINCT makes every row unique again, so it returns one row per customer.

questions.stem: HAVING differs from WHERE because HAVING:
options: Filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before it
Is required whenever GROUP BY is used
Filters rows before aggregation, whereas WHERE filters afterwards
Can only be used with ORDER BY
questions.explanation: (C) is the same statement inverted — the most common way this is got wrong — and GROUP BY is perfectly valid without HAVING.

questions.stem: Normalisation reduces redundancy but imposes which cost on analytical queries?
options: More joins are required, which slows large aggregate queries
Values can no longer be validated on entry
Primary keys must be recreated for every table
Referential integrity can no longer be enforced
questions.explanation: This is exactly why analytical warehouses are deliberately denormalised into star schemas — the trade is storage and redundancy against query speed.

questions.stem: In an ERD, a crow's foot with a circle at the CUSTOMER end of a CUSTOMER–ORDER relationship indicates:
options: One and only one customer per order
Zero or many customers per order
Exactly one order per customer
Zero or one customer per order
questions.explanation: Crow's foot = many, circle = optional (zero). A single perpendicular bar means one, and a bar plus circle means zero or one — which is (D) and the closest distractor.

questions.stem: A flat file storing customer name and address alongside every order suffers primarily from:
options: Referential integrity failure, since there is no foreign key
Insufficient validation on the address field
An inability to sort records by customer
Update anomalies, because one address change must be applied consistently to many rows
questions.explanation: The defect is redundancy producing update, insert and delete anomalies. There is no referential integrity to fail because there are no relationships, which is why (A) is subtly wrong.

questions.stem: A composite key is required when:
options: The primary key value may change over time
The table contains more than one foreign key
The table participates in a one-to-many relationship
No single attribute uniquely identifies a record
questions.explanation: Multiple foreign keys (B) are common without needing a composite key — for example an ORDER table referencing both CUSTOMER and EMPLOYEE.

questions.stem: =VLOOKUP(B2, Stock!A:D, 4, TRUE) returns unexpected values. The most likely cause is:
options: The lookup column is not the leftmost column of the range
Column 4 does not exist in the range
TRUE requests an approximate match on data that is not sorted ascending
The range spans a different worksheet
questions.explanation: Approximate match silently returns the nearest lower value, so on unsorted data it produces wrong answers without any error message — the quietest and most dangerous spreadsheet fault. (A) would raise an error, and (B) and (D) are valid here.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet feature is best suited to answering "what discount rate produces a $50,000 margin?"
options: Goal Seek
Conditional formatting
A pivot table
Data validation
questions.explanation: Goal Seek — works backwards from a target result to the required input. A pivot table summarises what already exists rather than solving for an unknown.

questions.stem: A data dictionary is most valuable because it:
options: Stores a backup copy of the table contents
Documents the physical location of each server
Records the meaning, type, format, validation rule and purpose of each field for future maintainers
Enforces referential integrity across the database
questions.explanation: It is documentation, not enforcement — the DBMS enforces the rules, the dictionary explains what CUST_STAT_3 actually means years later.

questions.stem: A DBMS can guarantee all of the following except:
options: That a foreign key value matches an existing primary key
That the recorded address is where the customer actually lives
That a date field contains a valid date
That two users editing the same record do not overwrite each other
questions.explanation: Structural correctness is enforceable; truth is not. A perfectly formatted, referentially valid address can still be the wrong address.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The strongest argument for on-premises rather than cloud storage in a specific enterprise is usually:
options: Cloud storage cannot be encrypted
A legal or contractual requirement that data remain within a specified jurisdiction
On-premises storage is cheaper at every scale
Cloud providers cannot guarantee availability
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty and sector-specific hosting rules are the usual decisive factor. Cost (C) generally favours cloud at variable scale, and major providers offer availability guarantees.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: Data sovereignty creates risk for an Australian enterprise because:
options: Overseas storage automatically breaches the Privacy Act
Data stored overseas cannot be encrypted in transit
Data stored overseas is subject to that country's laws regardless of the Australian contract
Data cannot be retrieved once it leaves Australia
questions.explanation: Cross-border disclosure is permitted under APP 8 with conditions — so (A) overstates it — but the foreign legal reach over the stored copy is the exposure that cannot be contracted away.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: Under APP 6, using data collected for order fulfilment to build a health-risk profile requires:
options: Notification to the OAIC within 30 days
Nothing further, since the data was lawfully collected
Only that the data be de-identified first
Fresh consent, because it is a secondary purpose the individual would not reasonably expect
questions.explanation: De-identification (C) is a mitigation but does not by itself authorise an unrelated secondary use, and (A) confuses APP 6 with the NDB scheme.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The NDB scheme is triggered by:
options: Any unauthorised access to personal information
Any loss of data, including accidental deletion of backups
An eligible data breach likely to result in serious harm
A breach affecting more than 1,000 individuals
questions.explanation: The threshold is likelihood of serious harm, not a record count (D) and not every access event (A) — a breach promptly remediated so harm is unlikely may not be notifiable.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, in force since 10 June 2025, differs from the Privacy Act because it:
options: Is enforced exclusively by the OAIC
Gives individuals a direct right to sue, including against entities not covered by the APPs
Applies only to Commonwealth agencies
Replaces the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme
questions.explanation: It covers intrusion upon seclusion and misuse of information, and its reach beyond APP entities is precisely what makes it significant for small business.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: From 10 December 2026, Australian privacy policies must disclose the use of automated decision-making that:
options: Involves any machine learning model
Processes more than 10,000 records
Operates without a human in the loop
Significantly affects an individual's rights or interests
questions.explanation: The trigger is the consequence for the individual, not the technique used (A) or the scale (B) — an ML model that recommends a playlist is out of scope.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The CARE principles complement FAIR principles because CARE is:
options: People- and purpose-oriented, addressing collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics
Concerned only with data retention periods
A legislative instrument enforceable by the OAIC
Technical, focusing on machine-readability
questions.explanation: FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) is the technical half; CARE addresses governance and rights, particularly for Indigenous data.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: De-identified data can sometimes be re-identified because:
options: Encryption keys are frequently leaked
Combinations of quasi-identifiers such as postcode, birth date and sex are often unique
De-identification is reversible with the original salt
Metadata is never removed during de-identification
questions.explanation: Linkage attacks exploit the uniqueness of attribute combinations — which is why small-cell suppression and aggregation thresholds accompany de-identification.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: Which is a supervised learning task?
options: Predicting next month's churn using accounts labelled churned or retained
An agent learning a warehouse routing policy through trial and error
Reducing 200 features to 10 principal components
Segmenting website visitors into behavioural groups
questions.explanation: Labels are the defining requirement. (D) is unsupervised, (C) is unsupervised dimensionality reduction, and (B) is reinforcement learning.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The validation set differs from the test set because the validation set is used to:
options: Confirm the final model's performance for reporting
Detect data entry errors before training
Tune model settings and compare candidate models during development
Train the model's weights
questions.explanation: The test set is touched once, at the end. Using it repeatedly to choose between models leaks information and inflates the reported performance.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: A model scores 98% on training data and 62% on unseen data. The diagnosis is:
options: Underfitting — the model is too simple
Overfitting — the model learned noise specific to the training set
Data drift — the world changed after deployment
Class imbalance — one outcome dominates the labels
questions.explanation: The gap between the two scores is the signature. Underfitting would give poor performance on both, and drift describes degradation after deployment rather than at evaluation.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: A deployed model's accuracy declines over 18 months although the code is unchanged. The cause is most likely:
options: Data drift — the distribution of incoming data has shifted
Overfitting introduced during the original training
A referential integrity failure in the source database
Insufficient validation data at training time
questions.explanation: Drift is why a deployed model is an operating commitment requiring monitoring and scheduled retraining, not a finished artefact.

questions.topic: Storage, law, ethics and machine learning
questions.stem: The claim "the model is objective because it removes human judgement" is best rebutted by pointing out that:
options: Human judgement is embedded in the choice of data, features, labels and success metric
All models require a human to approve each prediction
Models cannot process categorical variables
Objectivity requires a sample larger than any real dataset
questions.explanation: Automation does not remove those judgements — it launders them into apparent neutrality and applies them at scale.

questions.stem: A council publishes a dataset of noise complaints per suburb. Before drawing conclusions about which suburb is noisiest, the most important adjustment is:
options: Restricting the analysis to the most recent month
Removing outlier suburbs with very few complaints
Converting complaint counts to ordinal rankings
Normalising by population or dwelling count
questions.explanation: Raw counts across differently sized populations measure size as much as noise. (C) discards information without solving the problem, and (B) would delete exactly the quiet suburbs the comparison needs.

questions.stem: Two departments report different customer counts. The most likely root cause is:
options: One department's database has lost referential integrity
One dataset was collected passively and the other actively
The departments apply different business definitions of "customer"
One department is using a data lake and the other a warehouse
questions.explanation: Definitional divergence is the classic cause, and the fix is governance — a conformed, documented definition — rather than a technical repair.

questions.stem: A dataset used to set staffing levels was collected during a public holiday week. This is a failure of:
options: Relevance, since the period does not represent normal operating conditions
Reliability, since the method would not repeat
Accuracy, since the counts may be miscounted
Referential integrity, since the records lack a valid key
questions.explanation: The counts may be entirely accurate for that week — they simply do not answer the question being asked, which is what relevance means.

questions.stem: An enterprise proposes replacing all missing survey responses with the column average. The most significant consequence is:
options: The dataset can no longer be stored in a relational database
The records violate referential integrity
The data becomes ordinal rather than ratio
The mean is preserved but the variance is artificially reduced
questions.explanation: Mean imputation understates spread and can manufacture false confidence in later analysis — a subtle harm that a raw record count will not reveal.

questions.stem: A retailer claims its loyalty data proves customers prefer home brand. The strongest methodological objection is:
options: Loyalty data is qualitative and cannot support a preference claim
The sampling frame is the enterprise's own members, so it cannot speak for customers generally
Purchase data is passive and therefore unreliable
The dataset is too large for meaningful statistical inference
questions.explanation: (C) confuses passive collection with unreliability — passive behavioural data is often more accurate than self-report; its gap is motivation, not correctness.

questions.stem: After loading 4.2 million rows into a warehouse, the most important reconciliation check is:
options: That the target table has an index on the primary key
That the ETL job completed without a timeout
That the target schema is fully normalised
That source and target record counts and control totals on key measures agree
questions.explanation: A silent partial load is the dangerous failure — the job reports success and every downstream chart is quietly wrong. Job completion (B) does not prove completeness.

questions.stem: A model trained on applications from one metropolitan region is deployed nationally. The predictable failure is:
options: Poorer and potentially unfair performance for populations unlike the training distribution
Loss of referential integrity between training and deployment data
Reduced processing speed on regional data
The model reverting to its initial random weights
questions.explanation: It is dataset bias caused by an unrepresentative sample, and the mitigation is representative collection plus outcome auditing by subgroup after deployment.

questions.stem: An analyst reports "conversions up 400%". The single most important omission is:
options: Whether the data is nominal or ratio
The confidence interval around the estimate
The absolute base figures and the time period
Whether the data was collected actively or passively
questions.explanation: One to five conversions is a 400% increase and commercially meaningless. Percentages without a base are the classic misleading presentation.

questions.stem: The most defensible reason to keep the raw extract untouched and clean a separate copy is:
options: Storage costs less for raw files than for cleaned ones
The raw file loads faster into a warehouse
Reproducibility — cleaning decisions can be re-examined, reversed or corrected against the original
Raw data is exempt from privacy obligations
questions.explanation: Overwriting the raw file makes every downstream error permanent and unauditable. Raw data enjoys no privacy exemption — (D) is the dangerous distractor.

questions.stem: A supermarket infers pregnancy from purchase patterns and sends targeted offers. The core ethical objection is:
options: Purchase data is inaccurate for health inference
The inference reveals sensitive information the customer never disclosed or consented to reveal
Market basket analysis is not a valid statistical technique
The offers may be commercially unsuccessful
questions.explanation: Inference sidesteps consent entirely — the customer agreed to have purchases recorded, not to have a health status deduced from them.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes an analytics pipeline that discovers a data quality problem?
options: Collect → clean → store → analyse → discover the problem → return to collection or cleaning
Store → analyse → collect → clean → publish
Analyse → collect → clean → store → publish
Collect → clean → store → analyse → discover the problem → publish anyway with a caveat
questions.explanation: The pipeline is iterative. (D) is the tempting real-world shortcut and is exactly what a defensible process avoids.

questions.stem: An enterprise argues it needs no consent because the social media data it scraped was public. The strongest counter is:
options: Public data is always inaccurate and unusable
Public availability does not extinguish privacy obligations, and aggregation can create new sensitive inferences
Scraping is technically impossible at scale
Public data cannot be stored in a cloud service
questions.explanation: Scale and aggregation change the nature of the intrusion — a thousand individually public posts assembled into a profile is not equivalent to a thousand public posts.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports a claim that a cleaning process was well conducted?
options: A documented, repeatable log of each rule applied, records affected and the justification, with the raw file preserved
The final dataset is 20% smaller than the raw file
The cleaned dataset produced the expected conclusion
No records required modification
questions.explanation: (C) is confirmation bias presented as validation, and (B) measures deletion rather than quality.

questions.stem: An enterprise stores raw sensor data for 7 days and hourly aggregates for 5 years. This most directly demonstrates:
options: Tiered retention balancing analytical value against cost and privacy obligation
Referential integrity across storage tiers
De-identification through generalisation
ETL applied at the point of collection
questions.explanation: Aggregation here is a retention strategy. It may incidentally reduce identifiability, but calling it de-identification (C) mistakes a side effect for the purpose.

questions.stem: A dashboard's underlying source silently renames a field and the chart continues to render. The failure is one of:
options: Ongoing validation and change monitoring in the pipeline
Referential integrity in the source database
Sampling method selection
Data sovereignty compliance
questions.explanation: This is the most dangerous class of data error because nothing looks broken — no exception is raised and the visual is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes data integrity from data security?
options: Integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and consistency over the life cycle; security concerns protection from unauthorised access and harm
They are interchangeable terms
Integrity concerns who may access data; security concerns whether it is correct
Integrity applies to structured data only; security to unstructured data
questions.explanation: (C) is the definitions swapped, which is the intended trap — encryption protects confidentiality, not correctness.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to publish a dashboard of health outcomes by small geographic area. The essential precaution is:
options: Converting all measures to ordinal ranks
Suppressing small cells that could allow individuals to be identified
Restricting the dashboard to internal staff only
Storing the underlying data on premises
questions.explanation: "1 case, aged 15–19, postcode 2170" is identifying. (C) sidesteps the publication requirement rather than solving it.

questions.stem: Two variables correlate at 0.91. Before claiming causation an analyst should:
options: Increase the sample size until the correlation exceeds 0.95
Test for confounding variables, reverse causation and a plausible mechanism
Convert both variables to the same level of measurement
Re-run the analysis using the median instead of the mean
questions.explanation: A stronger correlation (A) does not become causal — the strength of an association says nothing about its direction or its cause.

questions.stem: The most persuasive evidence that a data-driven initiative succeeded is:
options: The dashboard was viewed 4,000 times
Stakeholders reported that the insights were interesting
The dataset grew substantially over the period
A measured change in the target metric against a pre-implementation baseline or control
questions.explanation: Views measure attention, not effect. Outcome evidence against a baseline is what an "evaluate" verb requires.

questions.stem: A dataset is described as accurate, reliable, valid and relevant, yet the conclusion drawn from it is wrong. The most likely explanation is:
options: The data was collected passively
The sample was too large
The data was stored in the cloud
The analysis or interpretation was flawed — RAVR describes the data, not the reasoning applied to it
questions.explanation: Good data does not guarantee good inference. This is why "interrogating" a result — aggregation, filtering, outliers, reasoning — is a separate skill from assessing the data.

questions.stem: Which action best addresses algorithmic bias specifically, as opposed to data bias?
options: Collecting a more representative training sample
Removing the protected attribute from the input data
Reviewing how features are weighted, selected and thresholded, and testing outcomes across subgroups
Increasing the size of the training set
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) address the data; (B) is the proxy-variable fallacy — suburb, school and career gaps can reconstruct the removed attribute.

questions.stem: An enterprise deploys an AI screening tool. Under Australia's Guidance for AI Adoption, the practice most directly engaged is:
options: Data minimisation at collection
Publication of the model's source code
Encryption of the model file at rest
Human oversight together with impact assessment and transparency
questions.explanation: The six practices are governance and accountability, impact assessment, risk management, transparency, testing and monitoring, and human oversight. Open-sourcing (B) is not among them.

questions.stem: A "human in the loop" control adds real protection only when the reviewer:
options: Sees every decision the system makes
Approves decisions within a fixed service-level time
Has the information, time, authority and incentive to disagree with the system
Has the same training as the model's developers
questions.explanation: A reviewer who rubber-stamps under time pressure adds the appearance of oversight — automation bias is exactly this failure.

questions.stem: The clearest example of selection bias created at the storage stage rather than collection is:
options: Cash transactions never being written to the transaction database
A survey distributed only through the mobile app
Interviewers unconsciously prompting a particular answer
An analyst choosing a flattering start date for a trend
questions.explanation: Records that are never captured create a systematic gap in the stored data. (B) is collection, (C) measurement and (D) analysis — the question tests where in the pipeline the bias enters.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to compare 2019 and 2026 customer satisfaction, but the survey instrument changed in 2022. The correct treatment is:
options: Compare the two periods directly, since both measure satisfaction
Convert both to ordinal ranks to make them comparable
State that the series is not directly comparable, and either restrict the comparison to a consistent period or document the break
Average the two instruments' results to smooth the transition
questions.explanation: A methodology break must be disclosed. (D) manufactures a continuous series out of two incompatible ones, which is worse than reporting the break honestly.

questions.stem: The best reason for an enterprise to prefer stratified over simple random sampling when the strata behave very differently is:
options: Stratified sampling always requires a smaller total sample
It guarantees subgroup representation and generally yields more precise estimates for the same size
It removes the need for a sampling frame
It eliminates response bias within each stratum
questions.explanation: Stratification needs a more detailed frame, not less — which rules out (C) — and it does nothing about how honestly people answer.

questions.stem: A dataset contains a field Gender with values M, F, Male, female, 1, 2 and blanks. The correct first step is:
options: Delete the field, since it is unusable
Impute the blanks using the modal value
Standardise the encoding to a documented scheme and record how blanks and ambiguous values were handled
Convert the field to an ordinal scale
questions.explanation: Standardisation with documentation preserves the information. Modal imputation (B) fabricates values on a nominal field where no "average" exists.

questions.stem: An enterprise argues blockchain would make its customer records "impossible to breach". The correct correction is:
options: Blockchain encrypts every record with the owner's private key
Blockchain removes the need for access control
Blockchain records cannot be read without consensus approval
Blockchain makes records tamper-evident, not confidential — it does not prevent unauthorised reading
questions.explanation: Integrity and confidentiality are different properties. Public blockchains are typically more readable, not less — which is why storing personal data on-chain is usually a poor decision.

questions.stem: Which combination best describes a defensible response to a dataset with known limitations?
options: Publish the headline figure without qualification to avoid confusing the audience
State the limitation, show uncertainty explicitly, and restrict the claims made to what the data can support
Delete the limited records and publish the remainder as complete
Delay publication until a perfect dataset becomes available
questions.explanation: (D) is the counsel of perfection that produces no decisions at all; (C) hides the limitation rather than disclosing it.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question on data collection for an enterprise, the strongest structure is:
options: Describe the enterprise's current process in detail
Define each collection method in turn, then conclude
Name the criteria, evaluate the methods against them with a specific example each, acknowledge limitations, then judge
List every method and identify which is most common in industry
questions.explanation: Definitions and descriptions cap at the lower bands; a criteria-based judgement with balanced limitations is what the verb demands.

questions.stem: A field storing Number of prior claims contains the value 0 for many policyholders. This confirms the field is:
options: Nominal, since zero is a category label
Ratio, since zero means a genuine absence of the quantity
Ordinal, since zero ranks below all other values
Interval, since zero is a point on a scale
questions.explanation: A true zero meaning "none" is the defining test for ratio. On an interval scale zero is arbitrary, which is why (D) fails here.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a data warehouse's ETL introduced an error rather than the source system?
options: The source and warehouse report different totals for the same period
The warehouse total matches the source only after a category mapping applied during Transform is reversed
The warehouse query runs slowly
The source system was updated after the load ran
questions.explanation: It isolates the fault to a specific Transform rule. (A) shows a discrepancy without locating it, and (D) offers an innocent explanation.

questions.stem: An enterprise measures "customer satisfaction" using average time on site. The problem is one of:
options: Reliability, since the measure would not repeat
Construct validity, since time on site may indicate confusion as easily as satisfaction
Accuracy, since timing may be imprecise
Relevance, since time on site is unrelated to the enterprise
questions.explanation: The measure is repeatable and plausibly related — it simply may not measure what it claims, which is the definition of a validity failure.

questions.stem: Which pair of terms is correctly matched?
options: Verification — checking a value is within an acceptable range
Validation — confirming the entered value matches the source document
Validation — confirming the value is factually true of the real world
Verification — confirming data was transferred or entered correctly
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are the two definitions swapped, and (C) overstates what validation can achieve — no entry check establishes real-world truth.

questions.stem: An analyst finds that a trend visible in every age group disappears when the groups are combined. This is:
options: An aggregation effect of the kind described by Simpson's paradox
A transcription error in the age field
A sampling error caused by small strata
Regression to the mean
questions.explanation: It is the strongest argument for asking at what level a figure is aggregated before accepting the conclusion drawn from it.

questions.stem: A junction table is given an extra attribute DateEnrolled. This is appropriate because:
options: Every table requires a date field for auditing
It resolves the many-to-many relationship
It provides a second candidate for the primary key
The attribute belongs to the relationship itself rather than to either entity
questions.explanation: A student does not have an enrolment date and a subject does not have one either — only the pairing does. (B) confuses the attribute with the table's structural purpose.

questions.stem: Which statement about cloud storage is false?
options: It can introduce data sovereignty exposure
It shifts responsibility for physical security to the provider
It converts capital expenditure into operating expenditure
It guarantees compliance with the Australian Privacy Principles
questions.explanation: Compliance remains the enterprise's obligation regardless of who runs the hardware — a provider's certifications support compliance but do not confer it.

questions.stem: A classification model is trained on 98% "not fraud" and 2% "fraud" records. Predicting "not fraud" every time yields 98% accuracy. The correct response is:
options: Accept the model, since 98% exceeds the target
Delete the majority class records until the classes are balanced in the test set
Convert the problem to regression
Recognise that accuracy is the wrong metric under class imbalance and evaluate detection of the minority class
questions.explanation: (B) is the trap — rebalancing the test set distorts the measured performance; sampling adjustments belong to training, not evaluation.

questions.stem: An enterprise publishes a dataset under a licence permitting reuse. Before republishing a derived visualisation, the most important check is:
options: That the file format is compatible with the charting tool
That the dataset contains no missing values
That the dataset is stored in Australia
That the licence permits derivative works and republication, and any attribution condition is met
questions.explanation: Permission to analyse is not automatically permission to republish — the ownership criterion in data integrity, and a Copyright Act 1968 issue.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between the 13 APPs and the NDB scheme?
options: The NDB scheme is a voluntary code and the APPs are law
The NDB scheme replaced the APPs in 2018
The APPs apply to government and the NDB scheme to private enterprise
The APPs govern ongoing handling of personal information; the NDB scheme sets obligations once an eligible breach occurs
questions.explanation: They operate together under the same Act — one is preventive and continuous, the other is reactive and event-triggered.

questions.stem: An enterprise runs a census rather than a sample. The remaining risk to representativeness is:
options: None, since every member is included
Non-response — those who do not participate may differ systematically from those who do
Sampling error, which grows with population size
Stratification error across subgroups
questions.explanation: A census eliminates sampling error but not non-response bias, which is why (A) is the intuitive but wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible use of a data lake?
options: Serving governed KPI definitions to executive dashboards
Storing only cleaned, conformed and aggregated records
Retaining raw multi-format data for exploratory analysis and future ML training, under a catalogue and access policy
Replacing the operational transaction database
questions.explanation: (B) describes a warehouse and (A) is what a warehouse or mart is for. Without the catalogue and policy the lake becomes a swamp.

questions.stem: A model's predictions are accurate but the enterprise cannot explain any individual decision to an affected customer. The most relevant obligation is:
options: Data minimisation
Transparency and, from December 2026, disclosure of significant automated decision-making
Encryption of the model at rest
Retention limitation
questions.explanation: Accuracy does not discharge the duty to explain. Contestability requires the affected person to be able to understand and challenge the decision.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of data that is reliable but not valid?
options: A survey with a 4% response rate
A well-standardised instrument that consistently measures brand recall while being used to report purchase intent
A dataset with several transcription errors
A sample drawn from a single suburb
questions.explanation: Consistent measurement of the wrong construct. (C) is an accuracy problem and (D) a representativeness problem.

questions.stem: An enterprise's ERD shows a 1:1 relationship between EMPLOYEE and LOCKER. The most likely reason not to merge the tables is:
options: Merging would violate referential integrity
1:1 relationships cannot be implemented in a relational database
The entities have independent life cycles — a locker may exist with no employee assigned
A composite key would be required after merging
questions.explanation: Optionality and independent existence are the usual justification for keeping a 1:1 split, along with security partitioning of sensitive attributes.

questions.stem: Which statement about hashing in a blockchain context is correct?
options: The hash of a block can be decrypted to recover the block's contents
Two different blocks will reliably produce the same hash if their sizes match
Changing a single character of a block's contents produces a completely different hash
The hash is recalculated only when the chain is audited
questions.explanation: The avalanche property is what makes tampering evident. (A) misdescribes hashing as encryption — the single most common error on this topic.

questions.stem: A dashboard is built directly on the operational OLTP database. The most likely consequence is:
options: The dashboard cannot be secured
Referential integrity will be lost
The data will become unstructured
The dashboard cannot display historical trends and may degrade transaction performance
questions.explanation: OLTP is normalised, current-state and tuned for many small writes — heavy analytical reads compete with the business, and history has usually been overwritten.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument that an enterprise should not collect a particular data field?
options: The field is difficult to validate at entry
The field serves no identified purpose, so collecting it adds privacy and breach exposure for no benefit
The field would increase the size of the database
The field is qualitative and therefore hard to analyse
questions.explanation: Data minimisation — data never collected cannot leak, be misused, or need to be secured, retained and destroyed.

questions.stem: An analyst uses MEDIAN rather than AVERAGE for household income. The justification is:
options: The median is easier to compute on large datasets
Income is ordinal, so the mean is invalid
The median is always closer to the mode
Income distributions are right-skewed, so the mean is pulled upward by a small number of very high earners
questions.explanation: Income is ratio data, so the mean is mathematically valid — it is simply less representative of the typical case, which is why (B) is wrong for the right-sounding reason.

questions.stem: A retailer's fraud model blocks a legitimate customer. The most appropriate governance response is:
options: Provide a human review path and a clear route to challenge the decision
Lower the detection threshold so fewer transactions are blocked
Retrain the model on the single blocked transaction
Disclose the model's full feature weights to the customer
questions.explanation: (B) trades one harm for another without addressing recourse, and (C) is overfitting to a single case. Contestability is the governance answer.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest instance of measurement bias?
options: Only app users are surveyed
A question worded "Don't you agree the new service is better?" leads respondents toward agreement
Records are deleted after 30 days
The analyst selects a favourable time period
questions.explanation: The instrument distorts the result. (A) is coverage/selection bias and (D) is an analysis-stage choice.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to test whether a new checkout increased conversion. The strongest evidence would come from:
options: Comparing conversion before and after the change
A controlled A/B test randomly assigning visitors to old and new checkouts
A customer survey asking whether the checkout felt faster
Comparing conversion against an industry benchmark
questions.explanation: Randomised assignment controls for seasonality, campaigns and composition effects that a simple before/after comparison (A) cannot separate out.

questions.stem: Which is not a legitimate reason to retain personal data?
options: An ongoing contractual relationship with the individual
A statutory record-keeping obligation
The possibility that a future analysis might find it useful
An active dispute requiring the record as evidence
questions.explanation: "It might be useful one day" is precisely the reasoning data minimisation and retention limitation exist to prevent — and it materially worsened the Optus breach's impact.

questions.stem: A model is described as unsupervised because it:
options: Is trained on data with no labels and finds structure on its own
Requires no human involvement at any stage
Runs without monitoring after deployment
Uses rewards and penalties rather than labelled examples
questions.explanation: (B) is the wording trap — "unsupervised" refers to the absence of labels, not the absence of people. (D) describes reinforcement learning.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of the relationship between OLTP and a data warehouse?
options: The warehouse replaces OLTP once it is built
OLTP records transactions as they happen; the warehouse integrates that history for analysis
OLTP is analytical and the warehouse is operational
They store identical data in different formats
questions.explanation: (C) is the pair inverted, and (D) ignores the integration, cleaning and historisation that ETL performs on the way through.

questions.stem: An enterprise cannot decide whether an unusual value is an error or a genuine extreme. The best next step is:
options: Replace it with the column median
Remove it and note the removal in the methodology
Trace the record back to its source to establish provenance before deciding
Report the result both with and without it, without investigating
questions.explanation: Investigation precedes treatment. (D) is a reasonable reporting practice but is not a substitute for finding out what the value actually is.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason a small retailer might reasonably reject a full data warehouse?
options: The build cost, ETL complexity and ongoing maintenance exceed the analytical benefit at that data volume
Warehouses cannot connect to visualisation tools
Warehouses cannot store historical data
Warehouses require on-premises hardware
questions.explanation: Right-sizing the solution is a legitimate judgement — a well-structured relational database plus a BI tool may deliver most of the value at a fraction of the cost.

questions.stem: A field contains the values 1, 2 and 3 representing Bronze, Silver and Gold membership. Calculating the mean membership level is:
options: Valid, because the values are numeric
Invalid, because the values are nominal and unordered
Invalid, because the codes are ordinal labels whose intervals are not equal
Valid only if the distribution is symmetric
questions.explanation: The tiers are ordered, so they are ordinal not nominal — (B) is right about the conclusion for the wrong reason, which is the trap.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a data mining technique to a business question?
options: Clustering — "Which customers will churn next month?"
Association — "Which products are frequently bought together?"
Classification — "What natural groups exist in our customer base?"
Regression — "Is this transaction fraudulent?"
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) are the pair swapped, and (D) describes a classification problem rather than a numeric prediction.

questions.stem: A "data swamp" arises primarily from a failure of:
options: Network bandwidth
Storage capacity
Governance — cataloguing, metadata, ownership and quality standards
Encryption at rest
questions.explanation: The technical platform is identical; what distinguishes a lake from a swamp is entirely a governance question.

questions.stem: Which action best supports the integrity dimension of a dataset over its life cycle?
options: Restricting access to authorised staff
Enforcing referential integrity, validation rules and version control on changes
Storing an offsite backup copy
Encrypting the database at rest
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) protect confidentiality and (C) protects availability — the three are routinely conflated in answers.

questions.stem: A model trained on ten years of hiring decisions reproduces historical under-hiring of one group. The most accurate description is:
options: Overfitting to the training data
A referential integrity failure
Class imbalance in the target variable
The model learned a real historical pattern, so the bias is in the data rather than the algorithm
questions.explanation: No explicit rule was written — the model faithfully learned what the data contained, which is what makes this harm so difficult to detect by inspecting the code.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to publish aggregate figures while enabling researchers to verify them. The best compromise is:
options: Publish the raw record-level data
Publish the aggregates together with the methodology, definitions and a controlled access process for the underlying data
Publish only the headline figure
Publish a de-identified copy with no methodology
questions.explanation: It balances reproducibility against privacy. (D) is the weakest of all — it carries re-identification risk and provides nothing to verify against.

questions.stem: Which best explains why a well-designed sample can beat a poorly designed census?
options: Samples are cheaper and therefore more accurate
A census with high non-response can be more biased than a small, properly randomised sample
Census data cannot be analysed statistically
Samples eliminate measurement error
questions.explanation: Coverage and non-response dominate. Cost (A) is a real advantage but does not by itself produce accuracy.

questions.stem: The clearest sign that an enterprise treats data governance seriously is:
options: The size of its data lake
The frequency of ETL refreshes
The number of dashboards published
Documented, agreed definitions of key measures with named owners and a change process
questions.explanation: Volume and activity are outputs; ownership and agreed definitions are the control that makes those outputs trustworthy.

questions.stem: A record shows a transaction dated before the customer's account was created. This is best caught by:
options: A presence check on the date field
A type check confirming the field contains a date
A cross-field consistency check comparing transaction date to account creation date
A format check confirming the pattern YYYY-MM-DD
questions.explanation: Single-field validation cannot detect it because both dates are individually valid — the error lives in the relationship between fields.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of using purchase history to measure customer preference?
options: It records what was bought given the available range, price and promotion, not what was preferred
Purchase data is qualitative
Purchase data cannot be timestamped
Purchase data is always incomplete
questions.explanation: Behaviour is constrained by what was on offer. Inferring preference from choice without accounting for the choice set is a classic interpretive error.

questions.stem: An enterprise applies k-anonymity so every combination of quasi-identifiers appears at least five times. This is an example of:
options: Encryption
Generalisation and suppression to reduce re-identification risk
Verification
Referential integrity
questions.explanation: It is achieved by generalising values and suppressing rare combinations — a privacy control, not a security or integrity one.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to document why a cleaning decision was made, not just what was done?
options: It is required before data can be loaded into a warehouse
It satisfies the Copyright Act
It reduces the file size of the cleaned dataset
A future analyst can judge whether the decision remains appropriate for a different question
questions.explanation: A rule that was right for one analysis may be wrong for the next — the reasoning is what makes the decision reviewable rather than merely repeatable.

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks for "all the data" to make a decision. The best professional response is:
options: Provide the full raw extract to avoid appearing to filter
Provide only the summary figure
Clarify the decision being made, then provide the relevant, quality-assessed subset with its limitations stated
Decline, since raw data cannot be shared
questions.explanation: Relevance is the first RAVR criterion for a reason. Dumping everything transfers the analytical burden without transferring the context needed to handle it.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of data being accurate but not relevant?
options: A survey with leading question wording
Correctly recorded 2019 foot traffic used to plan 2026 staffing
Miskeyed transaction amounts in the current ledger
A sample drawn only from loyalty members
questions.explanation: The figures are correct for what they measure; they simply do not bear on the question asked. (C) is accuracy, (A) validity, (D) representativeness.

questions.stem: In a relational schema, storing a customer's suburb, state and postcode in the ORDER table alongside the CustomerID is:
options: Redundant, creating update anomalies if the customer moves
Necessary for the order to be validated
A composite key
Required for referential integrity
questions.explanation: The address is an attribute of the customer, not of the order — unless it is deliberately snapshotted as the delivery address, which would be a different, justified design.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible reason to keep a model simple rather than maximise accuracy?
options: Simple models always generalise better
Complex models cannot be deployed on the cloud
Simple models require no test data
The decision must be explained to those affected, and explainability is a stated criterion
questions.explanation: (A) overstates a real tendency into a rule. The defensible argument is that explainability is itself a requirement, not a consolation prize.

questions.stem: An enterprise's data breach exposes records of customers who left six years ago. The clearest governance failure is:
options: Insufficient encryption strength
Absence of multi-factor authentication
Retention beyond the period for which the data served any purpose
Storing data offshore
questions.explanation: Access controls are important, but the records should not have been available to expose at all — which is what makes retention the primary failure.

questions.stem: Which statement about active and passive collection is correct?
options: Active collection generally yields smaller, consented, context-rich datasets; passive yields larger behavioural datasets without motivation
Passive collection produces only unstructured data
Active collection cannot be computerised
Passive collection always breaches privacy law
questions.explanation: Passive collection is lawful with proper notice and purpose — (D) is the overreach, and the manual/computerised axis is independent of active/passive, ruling out (C).

questions.stem: An analyst wants to justify a sampling method in an exam answer. The strongest structure is:
options: Describe the sample size calculation
Define all five sampling methods
State which method is most commonly used in industry
Name the method, explain how it addresses the specific representativeness risk in this population, and say why the alternatives are worse here
questions.explanation: "Justify" requires the rejection of alternatives — that element is what separates a justification from a description.

questions.stem: A dataset's provenance is unknown. The most serious consequence is:
options: It cannot be loaded into a spreadsheet
It cannot be visualised
Its accuracy, methodology, licensing and currency cannot be assessed, so no conclusion drawn from it is defensible
It must be encrypted before use
questions.explanation: Provenance underpins every other quality judgement — without it, RAVR cannot be applied at all.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes anomaly detection from classification?
options: Anomaly detection flags deviation from a learned norm, often without labelled examples of the rare event
Classification cannot be applied to fraud
Anomaly detection requires labelled examples of every anomaly type
They are the same technique under different names
questions.explanation: This matters practically: novel fraud has no historical label, so a purely supervised classifier cannot detect a pattern it has never seen.

questions.stem: An enterprise reports that its dashboard "uses live data". The most important follow-up question is:
options: Whether the data is stored in the cloud
Which charting library was used
How many people view the dashboard
What the actual refresh interval and source latency are, and what happens when the feed fails
questions.explanation: "Live" is a marketing word. A dashboard silently serving stale data because a feed failed is worse than one that shows nothing.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest concluding judgement in an extended response on an enterprise's data practices?
options: "The enterprise collects a large amount of data."
"Data practices should always be improved."

"Assessed against the criteria of data quality, privacy compliance and decision value, the practices are partly effective — RAVR is well addressed through documented cleaning and cross-validation, but retention beyond purpose and undisclosed automated decision-making create legal exposure from December 2026, so the recommendation is a retention schedule and an ADM disclosure before that date."
"The enterprise complies with the Privacy Act."
questions.explanation: Criteria named, evidence on both sides, a limitation identified, and a specific dated recommendation. The others are description, platitude or an unsupported assertion.
